What does Manton say is required for a person to attain true blessedness?

Manton teaches that true blessedness is attained only when the teaching of God prevails upon the heart and completely fills it, and that seeking blessedness in temporal things is a serious error. He warns that "It is not only an affront put upon God, but also a great wrong, to neglect the word of God, and the way he prescribes, and to seek blessedness in temporal things." Moreover, he explains that "That which fills must be greater than the thing filled," indicating that only the infinite fullness of God can satisfy the chaotic desires of the human heart.

What does Richard Mather say true joining to the church involves, as opposed to merely hearing the Word or having affection for the congregation?

Richard Mather teaches that true joining to the church is not simply dwelling in the town, hearing the Word, or expressing affection, but requires a voluntary covenantal fellowship. He explains that “it must be meant of joyning in that neere relation of Church-fellowship amongst them, so as to be engaged by volun tary consent and agreement to be members of their Church.” Thus, genuine membership is grounded in a conscious, covenantal agreement rather than mere attendance or emotional approval.

How does Watson contrast Christ's opening of the Sermon on the Mount with the giving of the Law on Sinai?

Watson teaches that Christ begins the Sermon on the Mount with promises and blessings rather than with commands and threatenings. Where the Law on the mount came with trumpet, flame, quaking earth, and fear, the Saviour whose lips dropped as the honeycomb opens with sweet, ravishing doctrine that draws even hard hearts.

Why does Manton say Christians should highly esteem the Lord's Prayer, and are they absolutely tied to its exact form?

Manton teaches that the Lord's Prayer was formed and indited by Christ, who as the wisdom of God knew both our necessities and the Father's good-will, and so gave a perfect form and directory. He adds that believers are not absolutely tied to that form; the apostles' recorded prayers do not show them using it as a fixed liturgy.

meta.passage:

   prayer; let me now come to the Lord's Prayer itself. This prayer was
   formed and indited by Christ, and therefore to be highly esteemed by
   Christians: Jesus Christ, who was the wisdom of God, he knew both our
   necessities and the Father's good-will towards us; and therefore surely
   he would give us a perfect form and directory. We are not absolutely
   tied to this form. We do not read that it was ever used by the

What reason does Thomas Gouge give for believers to give alms of their possessions?

Thomas Gouge teaches that believers should give alms because doing so makes all things clean and sanctified for them. He writes, "Give alms of such things as you have, and behold all things are clean unto you:" and argues that this act aligns with the apostolic inference that charitable giving secures and sanctifies the rest of one's goods. Moreover, Gouge stresses that people are "Stewards, than Lords and Owners of this worlds goods; all is the Lords," so giving alms reflects proper stewardship and brings God's blessing.

According to Sibbes in Works Vol04, how should a person's particular calling relate to their love for God?

Sibbes teaches that love of God must be expressed through the specific duties and offices each person holds, not as an abstract feeling. He writes that the command to love God "must love God ' with all our mind^ with all our heart, with all our power and strength,' Deut. vi. 5 ; that is, in our particular places" applies to each individual’s role, whether magistrate, minister, or statesman, so that love is demonstrated in the performance of those responsibilities. Sibbes further asks, "How far doth thy activity, thy power, thy sphere, that thou canst do anj'thing, stretch ? So far must thy love ; and thou must shew thy love in all the powers and abilities that God hath fur'- nished thee with," emphasizing that love to God is discovered in action within one's calling.

What does Guthrie say the new principle of life requires regarding sin and obedience to God’s commands?

Guthrie teaches that the new principle of life, by the good hand of God, makes a person set himself against every known sin, refusing to allow any darkness a peaceful abode, and to "respect all God's known commands;" to "live godly, righteously, and soberly" while pressing forward toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. He illustrates this radical rejection of sin with the biblical admonition "If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee," and reminds believers that "What fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?"

Watson teaches that God is attentive to the motives behind human actions, rewarding sincere good intentions while punishing deliberate wickedness. He writes, "If there be but a good intention, God takes notice," and contrasts this with the statement that "God punifheth in‑tentional wicked nefs, and crowns intentional goodnefs." What does Durham describe as the nature of the union between Christ and believers?

Durham teaches that the union between Christ the Bridegroom and believers the Bride is a mutual giving in which neither party retains independent power. He explains that the Bridegroom has no power over himself when he is married to the Bride, and likewise the Bride has no power over herself apart from the Bridegroom. The consent that makes the union effective comes through faith in Christ’s word, illustrated by the invitation, "Behold I stand at the door and knock, if any man will hear my voice and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me". Thus believers are called to relinquish self‑mastery and be wholly at Christ’s disposal.

How does the sermon advise Christians to exercise their voting rights in civil elections?

The sermon teaches that believers should not abandon their citizenship but should vote responsibly, seeking God’s guidance and acknowledging accountability. It urges that they use the right of voting "in the sight of Almighty God," recognizing that they will be brought into account for their choices. Moreover, it reminds them that "we are our own governors, to a great degree," and therefore must exercise prudence and prayer to make a right choice.

According to the sermon, where was Moses when he prayed the words “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling‑place in all generations”?

Spurgeon observes that Moses was "in the wilderness; not in some of the halls of Pharaoh, nor yet in a habitation in the land of Goshen; but in a wilderness." He explains that from that remote setting Moses looked upon the traveling Israelites and lifted his eyes to declare that God had been their dwelling‑place through every generation.

meta.heading: [Sermon 46 — "The Glorious Habitation"]
meta.passage:
This first verse will derive peculiar interest if you remember the place where Moses was when he thus prayed. He was in the wilderness; not in some of the halls of Pharaoh, nor yet in a habitation in the land of Goshen; but in a wilderness. And perhaps from the summit of the hill, looking upon the tribes of Israel as they were taking up their tents and marching along, he thought, "Ah! poor travelers. They seldom rest anywhere; they have not any settled habitation where they can dwell. Here they have no continuing city;" but he lifted his eyes above, and he said, "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations." Passing his eye back through history, he saw one great temple where God's people had dwelt; and with his prophetical eye rolling with sacred frenzy, he could see that throughout all futurity the specially chosen of God would be able to sing, "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations."

Taking this verse as the subject of our discourse this morning, we shall, first of all, explain it; and then we shall try and do what the old Puritans called "improve" it; by which they did not mean improve the text, but improve the people a little in the consideration of the verse.

First, we will try to explain it somewhat.

What does Spurgeon teach about the relationship between the church's binding and loosing actions on earth and in heaven?

Spurgeon teaches that the authority exercised by the church in binding and loosing is effective both on earth and in heaven, for he writes, "What they have bound on earth is bound in Heaven. What they have loosed on earth is also loosed in Heaven." This shows that the decisions of godly assemblies carry heavenly weight, and that when genuine repentance is expressed the bond is loosed on earth and also in Heaven. He also highlights the power of a prayer meeting of two believers, citing Jesus' promise, "Again I say unto you, that if two of you," which demonstrates that even a very small gathering can invoke divine response.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1761 — "The Lord with Two or Three"]
meta.passage:
This being done, according to Christ's rule--justly, impartially, lovingly, with prayer--that which is done by a few men and women assembled here below, is registered in the court above. What they have bound on earth is bound in Heaven. What they have loosed on earth is also loosed in Heaven. It is a happy privilege when they can loose the bound one! When repentance is expressed, when the backslider is restored, when the Church has reason to believe that the work of the Spirit is truly in the heart of the offender, then the bond is loosed on earth and it is also loosed in Heaven. The meetings of God's servants for the necessary discipline of the Church are not trifling meetings, but there is a Divine Power in them, since what they do is done in the name of Jesus Christ their Lord. Oh, that Church Meetings were more generally looked at in this solemn light!

Next, we are introduced to the Prayer Meeting. In the 19th verse we read, "Again I say unto you, that if two of you," two of you, "shall agree on earth as touching anything that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of My Father which is in Heaven." It is a very little meeting. It could not be smaller to be a meeting at all. There are only two there, but they are two praying Believers. They are two of the Lord's own servants, whose great concern is His kingdom! They are two earnest persons who very greatly desire the prosperity of the Church. They are two of kindred spirit, agreeing in love to God and the Truth.

What does the sermon describe as the purpose and effect of the 'third blessing' of unction for a preacher’s walk and ministry?

The sermon teaches that the third blessing, unction, is intended to anoint a minister not only in thought but in action, so that his daily walk and conversation become "gracious and useful" and leave a visible imprint of divine grace. It emphasizes that the minister should "Let him dip his foot in oil," meaning that the oil of the Holy Spirit should be upon the foot with which he moves, providing an "unquestioned office, enjoys an unfailing freshness, and exercises an effectual influence" wherever he goes. By having oil on the foot, the preacher’s footsteps become a testimony of grace, fulfilling the promise that "He shall dip his foot in oil."

meta.heading: [Sermon 2062 — "Shoes of Iron, and Strength Sufficient: A New Year's Promise"]
meta.passage:
We do not wish to be acceptable to the worldly wise, nor to the error-hunters of the day; but we are very anxious to be pleasant to the Lord's own children'our brethren in Christ. They have a holy taste whereby they discern spiritual meats, and we would bring forth for food that which they will account to be nourishing and savoury. Every minister prays to be "acceptable to his brethren."

And what could we do without the third blessing, namely that of unction? "Let him dip his foot in oil." Oh, for an anointing of the Holy Spirit, not only upon the head with which we think, but upon the foot with which we move! We would have our daily walk and conversation gracious and useful. We wish that, wherever we go, we may leave behind us the print of divine grace. I was asking concerning a preacher what kind of man he was, and the simple, humble cottager, answered me, "Well, sir, he is this kind of man: if he comes to see you, you know that he has been." We must not only have oil in the lamps of our public ministry, but oil in the vessels of our private study. We need the holy oil everywhere, upon every garment, even down to our skirts. I know that there are mockers who scoff at the very mention of unction; but I pray that to myself and my brethren the promise may be fulfilled, "He shall dip his foot in oil." Such a man, anointed with fresh oil, holds an unquestioned office, enjoys an unfailing freshness, and exercises an effectual influence. Wherever he goes you see his footprints, for his foot has been dipped in oil.

How does Sermon 116 describe the relationship between sins we notice and the secret sins we are unaware of?

Spurgeon teaches that the sins we notice are only a small portion of our total unholiness, comparing them to “the farmer's small samples which he brings to market, when he has left his granary full at home.” He asserts that “sin is sin, whether we see it or not,” so secret sins are just as real, though they lack the aggravation of willfulness.

meta.heading: [Sermon 116 — "Secret Sins"]
meta.passage: Why, if we could receive pardon for all our sins by telling every sin we have committed in one hour, there is not one of us who would be able to enter heaven, since, besides the sins that are known to us and that we may be able to confess, there are a vast mass of sins, which are as truly sins as those which we do observe, but which are secret, and come not beneath our eye. Oh! if we had eyes like those of God, we should think very differently of ourselves. The sins that we see and confess are but like the farmer's small samples which he brings to market, when he has left his granary full at home. We have but a very few sins which we can observe and detect, compared with those which are hidden to ourselves and unseen by our fellow creatures. I doubt not it is true of all of us who are here, that in every hour of our existence in which we are active, we commit tens of thousands of unholinesses for which conscience has never reproved us, because we have never seen them to be wrong, seeing we have not studied God's laws as we ought to have done. Now, be it known to us all that sin is sin, whether we see it or not—that a sin secret to us is a sin as truly as if we knew it to be a sin, though not so great a sin in the sight of God as if it had been committed presumptuously, seeing that it lacks the aggravation of willfulness.

According to Sermon 3060, what three prerequisites must a person meet before he can sincerely say, "The Lord is my Shepherd; I shall not want"?

In Sermon 3060, Spurgeon teaches that before one can honestly appropriate the Psalmist’s declaration, three prerequisites must be met: first, a person must recognize his own nature as that of a sheep, because "it is absolutely necessary that he should feel himself to be like a sheep by nature"; second, he must have experienced a past testimony of God’s care, as the sermon notes that a man "must have had some testimony of Divine care and goodness in the past"; and third, he must possess a holy confidence. Only when these conditions are satisfied can the believer sincerely proclaim, "The Lord is my Shepherd; I shall not want."

meta.heading: [Sermon 3060 — "The Good Shepherd"]
meta.passage:
"The Lord is my Shepherd; I shall not want." How naturally it seems to strike on the ear as uttered by David who had, himself, been a shepherd boy! He remembers how he had led his flock by the waters in the warm summer, how he had made them lie down in shady nooks by the side of the river, how, on sultry days, he had led them on the high hills that they might feel the cool air and how, when the winter set in, he had led them into the valleys that they might be hidden from the stormy blasts. Well could he remember the tender care with which he protected the lambs and carried them--and how he had tended the wounded of the flock. And now, appropriating to himself the familiar figure of a sheep, he says, "The Lord is my Shepherd; I shall not want." I will try to preach experimentally tonight and I wonder how many of you will be able to follow the Psalmist with me while I attempt to do so?

First of all, there are some preliminaries before a man can say this--it is absolutely necessary that he should feel himself to be like a sheep by nature, for he cannot know that God is his Shepherd unless he feels in himself that he has the nature of a sheep. Secondly, there is a sweet assurance--a man must have had some testimony of Divine care and goodness in the past, otherwise he cannot appropriate to himself this verse, "The Lord is my Shepherd." And thirdly, there is a holy confidence.

According to the sermon, what does the Lord say He has to break a hard‑hearted person's heart?

Spurgeon teaches that the Lord says, "but I have the hammer that can break the heart in pieces and make it fly into shivers!" He uses this vivid image to demonstrate that even the most stubborn, hard‑hearted individuals can be shattered by divine power.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2629 — "God's Work in Man"]
meta.passage:
I can shut it and no man can open it." "But suppose they should be hard-hearted and will not repent?" "Yes," says the Lord, "but I have the hammer that can break the heart in pieces and make it fly into shivers!" "But suppose they should be stony-hearted and will not melt?" "No," says the Lord, "but I have a fire that will melt the most adamantine rock that was ever known. Yes, that can consume the rock out of the heart and utterly burn it away." According to Spurgeon in Sermon 3486, how does he describe the seriousness of sin committed by a believer compared to the same sin committed by a non‑believer?

Spurgeon teaches that sin committed by a Christian is a far greater aggravation than the same sin committed by someone outside the faith, because “the nearer a man is to God's heart, the more detestable is the sin in him!” He warns believers not to treat sin lightly, urging constant vigilance: “Quick as the apple of an eye, O God, my conscience make! Awake, my Soul, when sin is near And keep it still awake.” Thus, the nearer one is to God, the more grievous the offense, and Christians must guard themselves carefully against it.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3486 — "God's Desire for Us, and His Work in Us"]
meta.passage:
I have been taught in my most secret places to know You, and yet for all that, I have revolted and gone aside, and committed this foul sin of adultery and murder." If so--if that is the correct translation (and there is no reason why that should not be correct, as well as the one we have here), it teaches us that it is a great aggravation to sin when sin is committed by a Christian. Never say that because a man is a Believer his sin is less! No, but if it is the same sin as in another, it is far worse in him than it would be in another! A stranger may say of me what my child must not say without being guilty of great ingratitude and much unkindness. It was you, a man, my friend, my acquaintance--this made the treachery of Judas to become so cutting to the Savior. The nearer a man is to God's heart, the more detestable is the sin in him! You cannot bear to see an evil in one you love. If one you love has a toothache, you think more of the pain of that beloved one than of some far greater sickness of one in whom you take no concern. So sin is a disease which, when God sees in His own beloved child, He perceives it with sorrow and He is quick to remove it and to heal it. Never trifle with sin because you are a Christian! Rather be the more careful to watch against it--

"Quick as the apple of an eye, O God, my conscience make! Awake, my Soul, when sin is near And keep it still awake."

What does Sermon 1224 say about the impact of human opposition on Jesus Christ?

Spurgeon teaches that human opposition does not diminish Christ’s glory or affect Him in any way; the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner and remains uninjured. He declares, "the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner" and adds, "Human opposition shall no more thwart the Divine will than a sere leaf cast into Niagara can block the water flow."

meta.heading: [Sermon 1224 — "Jesus, The Stumbling Stone Of Unbelievers"]
meta.passage:
He has already rejected God's Gospel--why should he respect the Law?

If the silken cords of love are broken asunder, how much less is the man likely to bear the bonds of law? Now, inasmuch as it is painfully certain that a very large proportion of these who hear the Gospel are unbelieving and disobedient, it becomes important to consider, What is the result of this disobedience? This disobedience leads them into violent opposition. What effect does their opposition produce? The text tells us the result of human opposition upon Christ Himself, and, secondly upon the persons who offer it.

Let us consider, in the first place, then, THE RESULT OF THE UNBELIEF AND THE OPPOSITION OF MEN AGAINST THE LORD JESUS CHRIST. We are told that, as far as He is concerned, "the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner"--in one word, it has not affected Him at all! The opposition of mankind has, by no means, and in no degree, lessened the Glory which God has put upon His dear Son. The builders rejected the stone with disdain--"It shall not be built," they said, "in the temple of our hope."

But, God has said, "It shall be the top stone," and the top stone it is, and shall be, despite all the opposition of earth or Hell. The rage of puny man shall no more defeat the Lord than the anger of a gnat can affect the sun! Human opposition shall no more thwart the Divine will than a sere leaf cast into Niagara can block the water flow. He that stumbles upon this stone shall be broken, but the stone itself will not be injured.

What reason does Spurgeon give in Sermon 1291 for why bearing the yoke in youth is advantageous?

Spurgeon teaches that submitting to God's yoke while still young prepares a person for a life of useful service, just as a young animal must be broken early to become a reliable worker. He explains that the burden may be uncomfortable, but it is profitable, and illustrates the point by noting that "If the bullock is not broken when it is young, it will never make a good plowing ox." By being “broken” in youth, believers develop the strength and obedience needed for later ministry.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1291 — "The Best Burden for Young Shoulders"]
meta.passage:
No, much more--we ought to be thankful for all His appointments even when they displease the flesh--being quite certain that His will is the best that can be and that if we could see the end from the beginning it is exactly what we should choose if we were as wise and good as our heavenly Father is. Our shoulders bow themselves with gladness to the burden which Jesus declares to be profitable to us! This assurance from His lips makes His yoke easy to bear. Our text tells us of something which, though not very comfortable, is good--"It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his

youth!"

The illustration is drawn from cattle. The bullocks have to bear the yoke. They go in pairs and the yoke is borne upon their shoulders. The yoke is somewhat burdensome. If the bullock is not broken when it is young, it will never make a good plowing ox. It will be fretted and troubled with the labor it will have to do. It will be very hard work to drive it and the farmer will accomplish but little plowing. It is good for the bullock to be brought into subjection while it is young--and so it is with all sorts of animals--the horse must be broken while he is a colt. And if a certain period of that horse's life is allowed to pass over without its being under the trainer's hand, it will never make a thoroughly useful horse.

If you want to train a dog you must take him while he is young and teach him his work. That is the metaphor. It is just so with men. It is good for us that we are broken while we are yet young and learn to bear the yoke in our youth.

What does the sermon say is the basis for God’s mercy toward Israel even though she is described as unrepentant and sinful?

The sermon teaches that God’s mercy is grounded in the "strange dispensations of Divine Grace" rather than any merit on Israel’s part. It points out that the introductory word "therefore" signals a conclusion of mercy drawn from the context, even though the Prophet describes Israel with terms of "whoredom" and "uncleanness" and notes that "they speak not of her goodness, but of her badness." Thus, the singular reason for divine grace is the sovereign grace itself, not Israel’s repentance.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2754 — "Strange Dispensations and Matchless Consolations"]
meta.passage:
''Therefore, behold!" I see, in the next place, the strange dispensations of Divine Grace. "I will bring her into the wilderness." In the third place, matchless consolations. "I will speak comfortably to her." And, in the fourth place, sweet persuasions.' 'I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably to her."

In the first place, we have, in our text, THE SINGULAR REASONS FOR DIVINE GRACE. "Therefore, behold!"

It is not without cause that the word, "therefore," is inserted here. We are to look to the context to find what are the premises from which a conclusion of mercy is drawn. You might naturally conceive, judging according to human logic, that the preceding verses described either Israel's goodness, or else her abject repentance if she has gone astray and rebelled. But, on the contrary, there is no mention of these things at all! They speak not of her goodness, but of her badness and, in fact, they speak so strongly that the Prophet uses terms that are never employed except after excessive iniquity. He charges Israel with whoredom and speaks of her as having committed uncleanness with many lovers. This is strong language and shows that he means to declare the excessive character of her sin and, instead of speaking of her as being a penitent, he declares that she was still impenitent. Notwithstanding many, many Providences and the hedging up of her way with thorns, she would break through and run after her many false lovers.

Why does Gill say that the knowledge of God is incommunicable to creatures?

Gill teaches that the knowledge of God is incommunicable because it is inseparable from God’s own nature: “it is his nature and essence, and therefore is incommunicable to a creature.” Since this knowledge is essential to the divine essence, no created being, even the human nature of Christ, can partake of it, and therefore it remains beyond the grasp of any creature.

How does Shedd argue that our moral feelings point to divine attributes in Dogmatic Theology Volume 3?

Shedd teaches that the awareness of our own moral feelings moves the mind toward the conception of divine attributes, noting that we are led “to the conception of the existence of attributes the same in kind, however exalted in degree, in the Divine Being.” In other words, the moral sense within humanity reflects a likeness to the moral qualities of God, though God's attributes are infinitely higher. This reasoning supports the broader claim that the order and constancy observed in nature reveal a unified, intelligent will governing the universe.

How does the author of the Institutes distinguish between God's will and His permissive allowance of evil, and what response is given to the charge that God becomes the author of sin by governing the counsels of the wicked?

The author of the Institutes explains that God’s sovereign will is not the same as His permissive allowance of evil; He permits evil "willingly" but does not will it as good, and He would not permit evil By emphasizing that the author shows that God’s governance of human counsels does not make Him the author of sin, as illustrated by the example of Absalom’s sin, where "God was pleased thus to avenge the adultery of David, he did not therefore enjoin an abandoned son to commit incest." Thus the objection that God is unjustly condemning men for obeying His decree is resolved by distinguishing divine decree from divine consent.

What reason does Dabney give for rejecting utility as the sole basis of moral obligation?

Dabney argues that moral obligation cannot rest on utility because conscience condemns secret sins that produce no outward loss, and he emphasizes that “the morality of the act is not in its utility, but in its rational motive.” He therefore concludes that virtue must be grounded in rational motives rather than merely in the usefulness of an action.

How does Gill describe the difference between God's truth and human truth?

Gill teaches that God's truth is unchanging and eternal, contrasting it with the mutable nature of human understanding. He states that “It is immutable and invariable, as he himself, as his nature is; truth does not always appear in the same light to men; at first more obscurely, then more clearly; it has its gradations and increase; but in God is always the same.” Thus, while human truth can appear in varying degrees of clarity, God’s truth remains constant, faithful, and true “yesterday, today, and for ever.”

What arguments does the author give for interpreting the antichrist in the passage as an ecclesiastical power rather than a civil one?

The author argues that several considerations point to an ecclesiastical interpretation. First, the designations "man of sin" and "son of perdition" are described as having a religious import, which makes them more appropriate to an ecclesiastical than a worldly power. Second, the antichrist is said to have his seat of power in the "temple of God," which the author explains is generally understood as the Church, indicating a tyrannical, usurping ecclesiastical authority. These reasons together support the view that the antichrist is an ecclesiastical power.
